n: A watchman sees a majestic warrior approaching from Edom, from its city Bozrah, in crimson-stained clothes. He answers, “It is I, speaking in righteousness, mighty to save.” D&C 133 applies this scene to Christ’s Second Coming in red apparel.

f.w: Who is this that cometh from Edom
Bozrah
f.g: A major city of Edom; “Bozrah” sounds like the Hebrew for grape harvest.

f.w: Edom
f.g: Israel’s longtime enemy; in the prophets it often stands for the world opposed to God (Isaiah 34:5-6; D&C 1:36).

n: Why are your clothes red, like someone who has been treading grapes in a winepress?

f.w: the winefat
f.g: Wine vat—a stone pit where people stomped grapes barefoot.

f.w: Wherefore art thou red in thine apparel

n: “I have trodden the winepress alone; no one was with me.” In context it describes judgment on the wicked, but Latter-day Saints also hear the Savior’s solitary suffering in Gethsemane, where He alone bore the full weight of sin.

f.w: I have trodden the winepress alone
of the people there was none with me

n: The day of vengeance was in His heart, and the year of His redeemed had come. Judgment on evil and redemption of His people come together.

f.w: the year of my redeemed is come

n: He looked, but no one helped; amazed that no one stepped in, His own arm brought salvation. Only the Savior could accomplish the Atonement.

f.w: mine own arm brought salvation unto me
I wondered that there was none to uphold

n: He trampled the nations in His wrath and made them drunk with His fury—the cup of judgment.

f.w: make them drunk in my fury

n: The tone shifts to a beautiful prayer of remembrance. The prophet recalls the Lord’s acts of loving kindness and great goodness toward Israel.

f.w: the lovingkindnesses of the LORD
f.g: Hebrew ḥasdei YHWH—the Lord’s acts of faithful covenant love.

n: God had said, “Surely they are My people, children who will not betray Me,” and so He became their Savior. His trust in His people was moving—and they would test it.

f.w: children that will not lie
f.g: Children who will not be false or disloyal.

f.w: so he was their Saviour

n: In all their suffering He suffered too, and the angel of His presence saved them. In His love and pity He redeemed them and carried them all along. God is not distant from our pain—He feels it with us. D&C 133:53 quotes this verse.

f.w: In all their affliction he was afflicted
the angel of his presence
he bare them, and carried them

n: But they rebelled and grieved His Holy Spirit, so He became like an enemy and fought against them. Paul warns not to grieve the Holy Spirit.

f.w: vexed his holy Spirit
vexed

n: Then the people remembered the days of Moses: Where is the God who brought them up through the sea with their shepherd? Where is He who put His Holy Spirit among them?

f.w: the shepherd of his flock
he that put his holy Spirit within him

n: Who guided Moses’s right hand with His glorious arm and split the sea before them to make an everlasting name?

f.w: dividing the water before them

n: Who led them through the depths as surefooted as a horse running on open ground, so they didn’t stumble?

f.w: as an horse in the wilderness
f.g: Like a horse on open, level ground—steady and sure.

n: Like cattle going down into a peaceful valley, the Spirit of the Lord gave them rest. So God led His people and made His name glorious.

f.w: the Spirit of the LORD caused him to rest

n: A plea: look down from heaven! Where is Your zeal and might? Where is Your deep tender compassion? Why are You holding it back from me?

f.w: Look down from heaven
the sounding of thy bowels
f.g: The stirring of Your inner feelings—in Hebrew thought the bowels were the seat of deep compassion.

n: You are our Father, even if Abraham and Jacob wouldn’t recognize us. You, Lord, are our Father and Redeemer; that has always been Your name. A rare and tender Old Testament address to God as Father.

f.w: thou, O LORD, art our father
Abraham be ignorant of us
f.g: Even if our ancestors would disown us, God will not.

n: Why did You let us wander and harden our hearts? Come back for the sake of Your servants. The question reflects Hebrew thinking that God is ultimately behind all events; it is also an honest cry of grief.

f.w: why hast thou made us to err from thy ways
f.g: Hebrew idiom often credits God with permitting what people choose.

n: Your holy people held the land only a short time; now enemies have trampled Your sanctuary—likely a reference to the temple’s destruction.

f.w: our adversaries have trodden down thy sanctuary

n: We have become like people You never ruled, never called by Your name. The plea: claim us again as Your own.

f.w: they were not called by thy name
